issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Reginald had been driving a bus for over two decades, and his daily routine had become second nature. He knew every route by heart, every stop, every nuance of traffic flow. But it was on one fateful night, five years ago, that his life took an abrupt turn. Reginald had stopped at a truck stop to refuel when he was attacked and brutally raped in the parking lot. The sounds of screeching tires and muffled voices still echoed in his mind like a perpetual nightmare. As time passed, Reginald found it increasingly difficult to shake off the memories of that night. Whenever he remembered the event, the same terror he felt at the time came flooding back. He would relive the fear, the helplessness, and the shame. His memories of the event were like a film reel playing over and over in his mind, with vivid images and haunting sounds. Reginald couldn't escape the feeling that he was somehow to blame for what happened. Reginald's perception of others had also changed dramatically since the incident. He now believed people couldn't be trusted; they were capable of unspeakable cruelty at any moment. This mistrust extended to his passengers, colleagues, and even family members. His faith in humanity had been shattered, leaving him with a deep sense of disillusionment. Reginald felt ashamed not only of what happened to his body but also for being vulnerable. As the memories continued to haunt him, Reginald started noticing subtle changes in his behavior. He became increasingly exhausted, partly due to lack of sleep and partly because he couldn't shake off the feeling of hypervigilance that had become his constant companion. Simple tasks like driving with others or navigating through crowded areas began to feel daunting. The sounds of screeching tires, revving engines, or even a loud voice made him jump. Reginald's relationships suffered as well. His wife, Sarah, noticed the change in him but struggled to understand what was happening. Reginald became withdrawn and isolated, avoiding social gatherings and family events. He felt like he was living in a constant state of fear, always on edge, waiting for the next attack. At work, Reginald found it increasingly difficult to drive with passengers, especially when they would start conversations or make loud noises. The cacophony of sounds and the anxiety it triggered made him feel like he was losing control. He started avoiding certain routes or altering his schedule to minimize interactions with others. His supervisor noticed a decline in his performance and expressed concerns about Reginald's ability to continue driving safely. Reginald knew something had to change, but he didn't know where to start. The memories still lingered, the shame still burned within him, and the fear remained ever-present. It was only when he received a letter from his supervisor stating that his job was at risk due to his performance that Reginald realized he needed help. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find some way to silence the perpetual film reel in his mind and learn to trust again. As he sat in the waiting room, flipping through magazines without really reading them, Reginald couldn't shake off the feeling of uncertainty. What if therapy didn't work? What if he would never be able to overcome this trauma? He took a deep breath, knowing it was time to confront his fears head-on and take the first step towards healing.
